questions.prompt: Which combination in an SMS is a classic phishing warning sign?

options.text: Urgent freeze threat plus a shortened or unfamiliar link
A reminder without any clickable links or pressure
options.explanationWrong: No link and no panic deadline is far less suspicious, though still verify in your app.

options.text: A message reminding you to open your official banking app yourself
options.explanationWrong: Directing you to open your official app independently is safe advice.

options.text: A message received during office hours
options.explanationWrong: Scammers send phishing texts at any hour.

questions.explanationCorrect: False urgency ('blocked in 2 hours') combined with a shortened link is the most common smishing formula.

questions.prompt: An SMS claims your bank KYC expired and asks you to tap a short link to update it. What should you do?

options.text: Tap the link just to see what the page looks like
options.explanationWrong: Fake lookalike pages are built to steal your login, OTP, or install malware.

options.text: Skip the link completely and open your bank's official app directly
Reply 'STOP' with your account number
options.explanationWrong: Replying confirms your number is active and never share account info by SMS.

options.text: Forward the link to family so they can test it
options.explanationWrong: Forwarding suspicious links puts others at risk too.

questions.explanationCorrect: Never tap SMS links for KYC or account alerts. Open your official banking app or website directly to verify.

questions.prompt: Why do phishing texts use link shorteners or lookalike web addresses?

options.text: To hide that the website does not belong to your real bank
Because banks are not allowed to use their own domain names
options.explanationWrong: Real banks always own and use their official domain names.

options.text: To encrypt your KYC documents faster
options.explanationWrong: Shorteners hide destinations; they do not make a fake site secure.

options.text: Because official bank apps cannot display KYC status
options.explanationWrong: Official banking apps have built-in KYC and account notice sections.

questions.explanationCorrect: Shortened links and slight misspellings mask fake credential-harvesting domains.

questions.prompt: After tapping no links and checking inside your official bank app that your KYC is active, what should you do with the phishing SMS?

options.text: Block the sender and report the phishing SMS/URL
Call the mobile number inside the SMS to scold them
options.explanationWrong: Calling scam numbers invites voice-phishing follow-ups.

options.text: Keep the link saved in case you need KYC later
options.explanationWrong: Delete or report it—never use an SMS link for banking.

options.text: Share your OTP on the helpline listed in the text
options.explanationWrong: Never share an OTP with any SMS sender or helpline.

questions.explanationCorrect: Blocking the sender stops repeat alerts, and reporting phishing texts helps telecoms and cybercells take fake sites down.

questions.prompt: A message asks you to enter a 6-digit OTP on a 'KYC verification portal' to prevent card suspension. What should you do?

options.text: Never share or enter the OTP—an OTP approves logins or debits, not KYC
Enter it if the page shows your bank's logo
options.explanationWrong: Logos and colours take seconds to copy onto fake sites.

options.text: Share only the first 3 digits first
options.explanationWrong: Never type any OTP onto an unverified link.

options.text: Ask the sender why they need an OTP
options.explanationWrong: Do not engage; verify directly inside your official bank app.

questions.explanationCorrect: An OTP is a live transaction or login key. Never enter it on links received through SMS or WhatsApp.

questions.prompt: Look closely at a sender ID like 'AX-BNKALRT' or a personal 10-digit mobile number sending bank threats. Why check sender details?

options.text: Random 10-digit numbers and strange prefixes often expose fake bank alerts
Because real banks only send KYC alerts from WhatsApp groups
options.explanationWrong: Banks do not demand urgent KYC updates via random personal numbers or chat groups.

options.text: Checking the sender automatically blocks the URL
options.explanationWrong: Inspecting the sender helps you spot red flags before you block and report it.

options.text: Sender IDs expire every 15 minutes
options.explanationWrong: Inspecting sender mismatches is a key clue, alongside checking inside the official app.

questions.explanationCorrect: Always check the sender, urgent tone, and links together—and verify any alert inside your real banking app.
